representative_system: Hadean ribozyme / mineral-pore replicator
self_sufficiency: Autocatalytic chemistry in vent pores (no cell membrane yet)
what_changed: Short RNA chains act as both template and rough catalyst, launching natural selection before cells exist.
source: Eigen (1971) Naturwissenschaften; Schrödinger (1944) What Is Life?; Agüera y Arcas et al. (2024) arXiv:2406.19108
plain_title: RNA strands copy themselves on warm mineral surfaces
plain_text: Short RNA chains in rock pores act as both the message and the copier, starting natural selection before true cells exist. Without proofreading, strands stay around 200 bits.
note: No Hadean fossils survive; anchored by lab ribozyme copying limits and early ocean habitability.

milestone: Cellular Binary Fission & Von Neumann Constructor
representative_system: LUCA / Escherichia coli dividing bacterium
self_sufficiency: 100% autonomous self-reproducing automaton from small molecules
what_changed: DNA tape + replisome copier + ribosome constructor let one cell build a complete second cell in ~20 minutes with ~10^-9 error.
source: von Neumann (1966); Hopfield (1974) PNAS 71:4135; Schrödinger (1944) What Is Life?
plain_title: One cell builds a full copy of itself in 20 minutes
plain_text: A DNA tape, a proofreading DNA copier and a protein-making ribosome let a single cell build a complete daughter cell from small molecules with about one mistake in a billion.
note: Reconstructed for the last universal common ancestor (LUCA); proofreading accuracy is measured in living bacteria.

representative_system: Stem eukaryote + alphaproteobacterial mitochondrion
self_sufficiency: 100% autonomous composite cell (host nucleus + dividing organelles)
what_changed: Two merged lineages synchronize replication: microtubules parcel packed chromosomes while captive mitochondria divide inside.
source: Lane & Martin (2010) Nature 467:929; Margulis (1970); Agüera y Arcas (2025) What Is Intelligence?
plain_title: Two merged cells learn to divide in step
plain_text: A host archaeon and its captured bacteria (future mitochondria) coordinate their division, using protein cables to pull packaged chromosomes apart cleanly.
note: Molecular clocks and early microfossils bracket the origin of nucleated eukaryotic cells.

representative_system: Bangiomorpha pubescens (multicellular red alga)
self_sufficiency: Autonomous multicellular life cycle via fertilized zygote
what_changed: Passing every new body through a single fertilized cell aligns clone interests and lets meiosis purge bad mutations.
source: Butterfield (2000) Paleobiology 26:386; Maynard Smith & Szathmáry (1995)
plain_title: Many-celled bodies restart from one fertilized cell
plain_text: Passing every generation through a single fertilized egg forces every cell in the new body to share the same genes, keeping tissues cooperative instead of cancerous.
note: Anchored by fossils of the red seaweed Bangiomorpha pubescens in Arctic Canada.

representative_system: Early Cambrian bilaterian metazoan
self_sufficiency: Self-assembling embryo via morphogen + bioelectric gradients
what_changed: Conserved Hox gene switches and bioelectric tissue fields stamp out modular segments, eyes, guts and appendages from one egg.
source: Erwin et al. (2011) Science 334:1091; Levin (2021) Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B
plain_title: Master body-plan switches stamp out modular segments
plain_text: Shared Hox gene switches and electrical gradients across embryos let one fertilized egg lay out heads, limbs, eyes and segments in repeatable order.
note: Cambrian body fossils and shared developmental toolkits across living bilaterian animals.

representative_system: Early vascular land plants & seed ferns
self_sufficiency: Dormant embryo + packed nutrient store + solar germination
what_changed: Encapsulating dormant plant embryos with food reserves lets reproduction cross dry continents and wait years for rain.
source: Kenrick & Crane (1997) Nature 389:33; Linkies et al. (2010) New Phytol.
plain_title: Tough spores and seeds pack an embryo with its lunch
plain_text: Wrapping a dormant plant embryo inside a weatherproof coat with stored food lets plants reproduce across dry land and wait years for rain.
note: Devonian spore and early seed-plant fossils from Rhynie chert and late Devonian strata.

representative_system: Early winged & holometabolous insects
self_sufficiency: One genome sequentially builds larva then dissolves and rebuilds winged adult
what_changed: Imaginal discs let one egg build a wingless eating machine first and a flying reproductive machine second without niche competition.
source: Truman & Riddiford (1999) Nature 401:447; Rosenberg et al. (2023) Sci. Adv.
plain_title: One genome builds two completely different bodies in sequence
plain_text: Complete metamorphosis lets an insect hatch as a wingless eating larva, then dissolve and rebuild itself from dormant disc cells into a winged adult.
note: Oldest holometabolous insect fossils and Carboniferous molecular-clock estimates.

milestone: Eusocial Queen Germline & Sterile Worker Castes
representative_system: Ant, bee and termite colonies
self_sufficiency: Colony-level reproduction (queen = germline, workers = extended soma)
what_changed: Separating egg-laying queens from millions of non-reproducing workers turns an entire insect society into one reproducing unit.
source: Hölldobler & Wilson (2009) The Superorganism; Maynard Smith & Szathmáry (1995)
plain_title: Whole colonies reproduce through a single queen
plain_text: Ants, bees and termites split reproduction from daily work: one queen lays eggs for decades while thousands or millions of sterile workers build, forage and defend.
note: Cretaceous amber fossils of early eusocial ants, bees and termites.

representative_system: Placental mammals & brooding birds
self_sufficiency: Biological reproduction + prolonged parental metabolic & behavioral provisioning
what_changed: Warm internal gestation and milk subsidize slow-maturing, high-neuron brains that finish wiring from experience after birth.
source: Herculano-Houzel (2016) The Human Advantage; Hrdy (2009) Mothers and Others
plain_title: Wombs, milk and long childhoods build slow-wiring brains
plain_text: Placental gestation and nursing pour energy into helpless young so large brains can wire themselves from years of lived experience after birth.
note: Rapid Paleocene radiation of placental mammals after the end-Cretaceous impact.

milestone: Percussive Stone Tool Manufacture & Social Copying
representative_system: Lomekwian & Oldowan hominin flintknappers
self_sufficiency: Exosomatic artifact made by biological hands (cannot self-replicate)
what_changed: Living minds begin manufacturing non-living functional artifacts whose designs replicate across generations by visual imitation.
source: Harmand et al. (2015) Nature 521:310; Stout & Chaminade (2007) Neuropsychologia
plain_title: Hands flake stone into tools that others copy by watching
plain_text: Early hominins strike stone cores at controlled angles to make sharp blades—the first manufactured objects passed down by social learning rather than DNA.
note: Dated volcanic ash layers bracketing the Lomekwi 3 stone tools in Kenya.

representative_system: Fertile Crescent wheat/barley & livestock domesticators
self_sufficiency: Human-steered biological reproduction of partner species
what_changed: Humans take over seed selection and animal mating, reshaping other genomes to multiply edible solar surplus.
source: Larson et al. (2014) PNAS 111:6139; Erb et al. (2018) Nature 553:73
plain_title: Farmers steer the breeding of crops and livestock
plain_text: By saving chosen seeds and pairing tame animals, people begin deliberately reshaping the genomes of wheat, rice, sheep and cattle.
note: Archaeobotanical grain and bone assemblages across the Fertile Crescent.

milestone: Phonetic Alphabet Compression & Bronze Piece-Mold Casting
representative_system: Proto-Sinaitic 22-letter script & Shang piece-mold bronze vessels
self_sufficiency: Human scribal & foundry template copying (~5 bits per letter)
what_changed: Compressing ~800 word-signs to 22 sound-letters democratizes scribal copying while ceramic piece-molds cast repeatable bronze vessels.
source: Goldwasser (2010) BAR; Bagley (1999) Cambridge History of Ancient China
plain_title: Twenty-two sound-letters and reusable bronze moulds
plain_text: Shrinking hundreds of word-signs down to two dozen phonetic letters makes writing far easier to learn and copy, while ceramic piece-moulds cast repeatable bronze vessels.
note: Proto-Sinaitic inscriptions and Shang Dynasty bronze foundry archaeology.

representative_system: Lydian/Greek iron coin dies & Panini's 3,959-rule Ashtadhyayi
self_sufficiency: Hardened metal dies stamp standardized tokens; formal rules compress language
what_changed: Engraved iron dies strike thousands of identical weight-certified coins per day while generative grammar compresses speech into exact rules.
source: Kiparsky (2009); Schaps (2004) The Invention of Coinage and the Monetization of Ancient Greece
plain_title: Hardened coin dies and exact rule-books for language
plain_text: Engraved iron dies strike thousands of identical weight-stamped coins a day, while Panini compresses Sanskrit into 3,959 generative rules.
note: Lydian electrum/silver coinage hoards and Iron Age textual chronology.

representative_system: Codex Sinaiticus & Late Antique monastery scriptoria
self_sufficiency: Hand-copied folded quires with page numbers & tables of contents
what_changed: Folding and stitching animal-skin sheets into numbered pages turns linear scrolls into durable, random-access reference books.
source: Roberts & Skeat (1983) The Birth of the Codex; Grafton & Williams (2006)
plain_title: Bound page-numbered books replace long scrolls
plain_text: Folding and stitching sheets into a codex lets a reader jump straight to any numbered page instead of unrolling metres of scroll.
note: Surviving Late Antique parchment codices such as Codex Sinaiticus.

representative_system: Samarkand–Baghdad rag-paper mills & Song Dynasty woodblock/clay type
self_sufficiency: Waterwheel pulp trip-hammers + carved woodblock template multiplication
what_changed: Linen rag paper drops writing-sheet cost tenfold across Eurasia while carved woodblocks and Bi Sheng's ceramic type print thousands of copies.
source: Bloom (2001) Paper Before Print; Tsien (1985) Science and Civilisation in China Vol. 5.1
plain_title: Water-powered paper mills and carved printing blocks
plain_text: Trip-hammer mills turn linen rags into cheap writing sheets ten times less costly than parchment, fueling woodblock and ceramic movable-type printing.
note: Dated Song Dynasty imprints and Islamic world paper-mill records.

representative_system: Gutenberg adjustable type mold & screw press (1450 CE)
self_sufficiency: Human-operated mechanical template replication (~300x cheaper copies)
what_changed: One steel punch and matrix cast thousands of interchangeable lead-tin letters, mechanizing accurate text replication.
source: Eisenstein (1979) The Printing Press as an Agent of Change; Hilbert & López (2011)
plain_title: Movable metal type mass-produces identical books
plain_text: Gutenberg's hand mould casts thousands of interchangeable lead-tin letters, cutting the cost of copying a book roughly three-hundred-fold.
note: Dated Mainz printing documents and surviving 1450s Gutenberg Bibles.

representative_system: Leibniz Stepped Reckoner, Pascaline & Philosophical Transactions (1665–1680)
self_sufficiency: Clockwork brass carry-gears mechanize arithmetic; journals replicate experiments
what_changed: Fluted brass drums automate carries across digits while printed journals publish methods so distant labs can reproduce every result.
source: Jones (2016) Reckoning with Matter; Kronick (1976) A History of Scientific & Technical Periodicals
plain_title: Brass gear calculators and peer-reviewed science journals
plain_text: Clockwork carry gears mechanize arithmetic while printed journals publish experimental recipes so distant laboratories can reproduce every test.
note: Surviving Pascal and Leibniz machines and 1665 Philosophical Transactions issues.

representative_system: Maudslay screw-cutting lathe, Jacquard loom & industrial assembly plants
self_sufficiency: Machines cut precision metal parts to build further machines (human-operated)
what_changed: Micrometer-accurate lathes and punched-card looms let fossil-fueled factories manufacture engines, telegraphs and more machine tools.
source: Hounshell (1984) From the American System to Mass Production; Agüera y Arcas (2025)
plain_title: Precision machine tools cut parts to build more machines
plain_text: Screw-cutting lathes and punched-card looms let steam-powered factories turn out interchangeable metal parts accurate to thousandths of an inch.
note: Industrial engineering archives from Maudslay (1800) and Jacquard (1804) onward.

representative_system: Hollerith 1890 census tabulator & Linotype hot-metal typesetter
self_sufficiency: Spring-loaded electric pins read binary paper cards at ~60 cards/min
what_changed: Punched cards turn population records and factory schedules into machine-sorted binary media.
source: Austrian (1982) Herman Hollerith; Beniger (1986) The Control Revolution
plain_title: Punched paper cards sort millions of census records
plain_text: Electric pins drop through holes in paper cards at 60 cards a minute, turning national censuses and factory schedules into machine-read binary data.
note: 1890 US Census Hollerith tabulator records and Linotype patents.

representative_system: ENIAC, Manchester Baby & EDVAC stored-program computers (1945–1949)
self_sufficiency: Software recipes copy and modify themselves in electronic memory at zero re-wiring cost
what_changed: Storing instructions in the same electronic memory as data lets one physical machine become any tool by loading a new bitstring.
source: von Neumann (1945) EDVAC Report; Goldstine (1972); Dyson (2012) Turing's Cathedral
plain_title: Software turns one electronic machine into any machine
plain_text: Keeping instructions in the same fast electronic memory as data lets a computer become a new tool in milliseconds without rewiring a single cable.
note: ENIAC (1945), Manchester Baby (1948) and EDVAC stored-program milestones.

milestone: Planar Silicon Photolithography & Cleanroom Wafer Fabs
representative_system: CMOS optical mask stepper & silicon wafer fab
self_sufficiency: Automated optical pattern transfer across global supply chain (not self-enclosed)
what_changed: Optical masks stamp billions of transistors onto silicon wafers in parallel—much like optical template replication—driving Moore's Law.
source: Noyce (1961); Moore (1965) Electronics; Mack (2007) Fundamental Principles of Optical Lithography
plain_title: Light stamps billions of transistors onto silicon wafers
plain_text: Optical masks project shrunk circuit patterns onto silicon wafers in cleanrooms, printing whole processors in parallel like pages on a press.
note: Planar integrated circuit inventions (1959–1961) and commercial CMOS steppers.

milestone: First Chemically Synthesized Living Cell & Billion-Phone CMOS
representative_system: Mycoplasma mycoides JCVI-syn1.0 (1.08-Mb synthetic genome, 2010) & smartphone SoC fabs
self_sufficiency: Digital computer file -> chemical oligonucleotides -> self-replicating bacterial cell
what_changed: A 1,077,947-letter genome typed on a computer and stitched from four chemical bottles boots up a living, dividing bacterial cell.
source: Gibson et al. (2010) Science 329:52; Hutchison et al. (2016) Science 351:aad6253
plain_title: A genome typed on a computer boots up a living cell
plain_text: Over a million DNA letters designed in a computer file are stitched together from chemical bottles and booted inside an empty cell into a dividing bacterium.
note: Published JCVI-syn1.0 synthetic Mycoplasma mycoides cell in May 2010.

representative_system: ASML EUV reticle scanner + benchtop DNA/mRNA synthesizers
self_sufficiency: Planet-spanning industrial constructor (~100,000-part EUV tool) + synthetic bio-fabs
what_changed: Laser-pulsed tin plasma prints 100B-transistor AI chips at nanometer scale while mRNA and DNA printers compile digital sequences into medicines and cells.
source: Levinson (2022) EUV Lithography; Karikó et al. (2005) Immunity 23:165; Hutchison et al. (2016)
plain_title: Extreme-ultraviolet light prints 100-billion-transistor chips
plain_text: Laser-blasted tin droplets emit 13.5-nanometre light to print modern AI chips, while benchtop synthesizers turn digital files into mRNA medicines.
note: High-volume EUV lithography deployment (2019–2020) and programmable mRNA vaccines.

milestone: AI-Assisted Chip Layout, Protein Design & Robotic Assembly
representative_system: RL chip floorplanners (AlphaChip) + generative protein/robot design
self_sufficiency: Recursive software/layout co-design; physical fab & mining still require human civilization
what_changed: AI models now help lay out next-generation AI accelerators, write software and design novel enzymes, closing part—not all—of von Neumann's constructor loop.
source: Mirhoseini et al. (2021) Nature 594:207; Watson et al. (2023) Nature 620:1089; Agüera y Arcas (2025)
plain_title: AI helps lay out the next generation of chips and proteins
plain_text: Learning systems now design chip floorplans, write code and invent working enzymes—closing the software half of self-design, though physical fabs still need a whole civilization.
note: Measured in 2021–2026 chip-design and de novo protein-design benchmarks.
